title: Fit for you
hook: judge every word and act that fits you, and don't be swayed by blame (Meditations 5.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: push it away. Your line was push it away. Which small troubling thought did you notice and set down? Day five hundred sixty-four.

There's always someone ready to comment. You start eating differently and a relative has notes. You speak up at a meeting and someone rolls their eyes. You give money to a cause and a friend tells you it's naive. Sometimes the critic is right, and it's worth listening. But often the right thing simply comes with a small crowd of people who'd rather you didn't. Marcus Aurelius, whose every public act had an audience, gave himself a rule for that crowd. Today: fit for you.
screen: `THERE'S ALWAYS SOMEONE WITH NOTES.` → `THE RIGHT THING HAS CRITICS.` → `FIT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the standard. Judge every word and act that is in line with nature, Marcus writes in the third entry of book five, as fit for you. In Stoic terms, in line with nature means in line with what a reasoning, social creature is made for: honest, fair, useful to others. That's the test, and it comes first. Second, the blame that follows. Don't let the blame or the talk of certain people that follows turn you aside. If a thing is good to do or say, he says, don't think it beneath you. Notice the order. You test the act first. Then, if it passes, the critics don't get a vote. Third, they have their own guide. Those people, Marcus says, have their own ruling mind and follow their own impulses. Don't keep looking over at them. That isn't contempt. It's simply that their mind is theirs to steer, and yours is yours. You can't hand your conscience to someone else's mood. Fourth, the straight road. Go straight on, he finishes, following your own nature and the common nature, because the road of both is one. What's right for you, done honestly, is also what's right for the whole. Here's the useful part. This rule doesn't mean ignore all feedback. Marcus elsewhere asks to be corrected, gladly, when he's wrong. The difference is the order. A critic with a reason gets heard, and maybe changes your mind. A critic with only disapproval doesn't get to decide what's fit for you.
screen: `JUDGE EACH ACT AS FIT FOR YOU.` · `DON'T LET THE BLAME TURN YOU ASIDE.` · `THEY HAVE THEIR OWN RULING MIND.` · `ONE STRAIGHT ROAD.` · then, large: `FIT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one right thing you've been holding back from because of a critic, real or imagined. Test it first, honestly: is it fair, true, useful? If it fails, let it go. If it passes, picture the critic's face. Let them have their own mind and their own opinion. Then picture yourself doing it anyway, calmly, without needing to win them over. The bell holds the time.
Fit for you. Marcus says test each word and act by nature; if it's right, it's fit for you, and the blame of others needn't turn you aside. Today's word.
Your line: fit for me. Do one right thing today that someone might criticize. Test it first, then don't wait for their approval. Day five hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.3 in two steps: first test an act for fairness and honesty, then, if it passes, don't let disapproval alone turn them aside.

original.note: Greek, 'according to nature': the Stoic test Marcus applies to every word and act in 5.3.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't care what people think.
what it means: test each act by nature first; if it's right, others' blame doesn't get a vote.
what a scholar hears: kata phusin, 'according to nature', the Stoic formula for the good life, joins your own nature to the nature of the whole.

notes: 5.3 paraphrased: judge every word and deed in accordance with nature to be fit for you; don't be diverted by the blame which follows from any people, nor by their words; if a thing is good to be done or said, don't consider it unworthy of you; those persons have their own ruling faculty and follow their own movement; don't regard them, but go straight on, following your own nature and the common nature, for the way of both is one. Confirm.
6.21: if anyone can show me that I do not think or act rightly, I will gladly change. Cited for 'asks to be corrected, gladly'. Confirm.
'Criticized for a living' is light shorthand for an emperor's public life; confirm tone.
Editor review (year 2, days 558–575): replaced the jokey unsourced 'criticized for a living'; softened the general claim about what all Stoics meant.
